﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾

﴿The Opening of the Book﴾

It is called al-Fatihah (the Opener), meaning the opening of the Book in writing, and with it the recitation in the prayer is opened.[^1] It is also called Umm al-Kitab (the Mother of the Book) according to the majority. Anas, al-Hasan and Ibn Sirin disliked calling it by this name. Al-Hasan and Ibn Sirin said: "That refers only to the Preserved Tablet." Al-Hasan said: "The clear verses (al-muhkamat) are the Mother of the Book." For this reason they also disliked calling it Umm al-Qur'an (the Mother of the Qur'an). However, it is established in the Sahih of al-Tirmidhi, which he also graded as sahih, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "al-Hamdu lillah is Umm al-Qur'an, Umm al-Kitab, al-Sab' al-Mathani (the seven oft-repeated), and the Great Qur'an." It is also called al-Hamd (the Praise), and it is called al-Salah (the Prayer), based on his statement (peace be upon him) concerning what his Lord said: "I have divided the prayer between Me and My servant into two halves. When the servant says, 'al-Hamdu lillahi Rabbi al-'alamin (All praise is due to God, Lord of the worlds),' God says: 'My servant has praised Me.'" The hadith continues. Al-Fatihah is therefore called "prayer" because it is a condition of the prayer. It is also called al-Shifa' (the Healing), based on what al-Darimi narrated from Abu Sa'id, traced to the Prophet: "The Opening of the Book is a healing from every poison." It is also called al-Ruqyah (the Incantation), based on the hadith of Abu Sa'id in the Sahih, when he recited it over the man who had been stung, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to him: "How did you know that it is an incantation?" Al-Sha'bi narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he called it Asas al-Qur'an (the Foundation of the Qur'an), and said: Its foundation is ﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾. Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah called it al-Waqiyah (the Protector). Yahya ibn Abi Kathir called it al-Kafiyah (the Sufficient), because it suffices in place of everything else, and nothing else suffices in its place, as occurs in some mursal hadiths: "Umm al-Qur'an is a substitute for other than it, and nothing other than it is a substitute for it."[^2] It is also called Surat al-Salah (the Surah of the Prayer) and al-Kanz (the Treasure), both mentioned by al-Zamakhshari in his al-Kashshaf. It is Meccan, said by Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah and Abu al-'Aliyah. It was also said to be Medinan, said by Abu Hurayrah, Mujahid, 'Ata' ibn Yasar and al-Zuhri. It is said that it was revealed twice: once in Mecca and once in Medina. The first view is closer to the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And We have certainly given you seven of the oft-repeated [verses]﴾ [al-Hijr: 87]. And God knows best. Abu al-Layth al-Samarqandi related that half of it was revealed in Mecca and the other half in Medina, which is very strange; al-Qurtubi transmitted it from him. It has seven verses without disagreement. ['Amr ibn 'Ubayd said it has eight; Husayn al-Ju'fi said it has six; these two are anomalous.] They differed only regarding the basmalah: is it an independent verse at the beginning of it, as is the view of the majority of the Kufan reciters, the consensus of a group of the Companions and the Successors, and a group of later scholars; or is it part of a verse, or not counted from its beginning at all, as is the view of the Medinan reciters and jurists? There are three opinions, and its explanation will come in its place, God willing, and in Him is trust.

They said: Its words are twenty-five and its letters are one hundred and thirteen. Al-Bukhari said at the beginning of the Book of Tafsir: "It is called Umm al-Kitab because writing of it begins in the mushafs and recitation of it begins in the prayer."[^3] It was also said: it is called that because the meanings of the entire Qur'an return to what it contains. Ibn Jarir said: The Arabs call every comprehensive matter, or every thing that precedes a matter and has subsequent things that follow it, of which it is the comprehensive leader, "umm." They call the membrane that encloses the brain "umm al-ra's" (the mother of the head). They also call the army's banner, under which they gather, "umm." He cited the verse of Dhu al-Rummah:

"Above his head is a mother for us, whose guidance we follow,
the gathering of affairs, and we do not disobey her command."[^4]

He means the spear. He said: Mecca is called Umm al-Qura (the Mother of the Towns) because it precedes all of them and gathers all others. It was also said: because the earth was spread out from it.

It is also called al-Fatihah because the recitation is opened with it, and the Companions began with it in writing the Imam Mushaf. Its naming as al-Sab' al-Mathani is authentic. They said: it is because it is repeated in the prayer, recited in every rak'ah, although "al-mathani" has another meaning besides this, as its explanation will come in its place, God willing.

Imam Ahmad said: Yazid ibn Harun related to us, Ibn Abi Dhi'b and Hashim ibn Hashim informed us, from Ibn Abi Dhi'b, from al-Maqburi, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said concerning Umm al-Qur'an: "It is Umm al-Qur'an, and it is al-Sab' al-Mathani, and it is the Great Qur'an."[^5] He then narrated it from Isma'il ibn 'Umar, from Ibn Abi Dhi'b with the same wording. Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari said: Yunus ibn 'Abd al-A'la related to me, Ibn Wahb informed us, Ibn Abi Dhi'b informed me, from Sa'id al-Maqburi, from Abu Hurayrah, may God be pleased with him, from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) who said: "It is Umm al-Qur'an, it is Fatihat al-Kitab, and it is al-Sab' al-Mathani."[^6] The Hafiz Abu Bakr Ahmad ibn Musa ibn Mardawayh said in his Tafsir: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Ziyad related to us, Muhammad ibn Ghalib ibn Harith related to us, Ishaq ibn 'Abd al-Wahid al-Mawsili related to us, al-Mu'afa ibn 'Imran related to us, from 'Abd al-Hamid ibn Ja'far, from Nuh ibn Abi Bilal, from al-Maqburi, from Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "al-Hamdu lillahi Rabbi al-'alamin are seven verses, the basmalah being the first of them. It is al-Sab' al-Mathani and the Great Qur'an, and it is Umm al-Kitab."[^7] [Then the chain's variant wording is given in the text.]

Al-Daraqutni also related it from Abu Hurayrah as a marfu' report, in similar or the same wording, and said: "They are all trustworthy (thiqat)."[^8] Al-Bayhaqi related from 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas and Abu Hurayrah that they explained the words of the Exalted ﴿seven of the oft-repeated﴾ [al-Hijr: 87] as referring to al-Fatihah, and that the basmalah is its seventh verse. The full discussion of this will come under the basmalah.

Al-A'mash narrated from Ibrahim who said: It was said to Ibn Mas'ud: "Why did you not write al-Fatihah in your mushaf?" He said: "If I had written it, I would have written it at the beginning of every surah." Abu Bakr ibn Abi Dawud said: He means wherever it is recited in the prayer. He said: "I was content with the Muslims' memorization of it instead of writing it down."

It has been said that al-Fatihah was the first thing of the Qur'an to be revealed, as occurs in a hadith narrated by al-Bayhaqi in Dala'il al-Nubuwwah.[^9] Al-Baqillani transmitted this as one of three opinions. It was also said that the first revelation was ﴿O you who wrap yourself [in garments]﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 1], as in the hadith of Jabir in the Sahih.[^10] It was also said that it was ﴿Recite in the name of your Lord who created﴾ [al-'Alaq: 1], and this is the correct view, as its explanation will come in its place. And from God is the help sought.

**Mention of what has been reported concerning the virtue of al-Fatihah**

Imam Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Hanbal, may God have mercy on him, said in his Musnad: Yahya ibn Sa'id related to us, from Shu'bah, who said: Khubayb ibn 'Abd al-Rahman related to me, from Hafs ibn 'Asim, from Abu Sa'id ibn al-Mu'alla, may God be pleased with him, who said: "I was praying when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) called me, but I did not respond to him until I had finished the prayer and came to him. He said: 'What prevented you from coming to me?' I said: 'O Messenger of God, I was praying.' He said: 'Did not God say: ﴿O you who believe, respond to God and to the Messenger when he calls you to that which gives you life﴾ [al-Anfal: 24]?' Then he said: 'I will teach you the greatest surah in the Qur'an before you leave the mosque.'" He said: He took my hand, and when he wanted to leave the mosque I said: "O Messenger of God, you said: 'I will teach you the greatest surah in the Qur'an.'" He said: "Yes: al-Hamdu lillahi Rabbi al-'alamin; it is al-Sab' al-Mathani and the Great Qur'an which I have been given."

Thus al-Bukhari narrated it from Musaddad and from 'Ali ibn al-Madini, both from Yahya ibn Sa'id al-Qattan, with this chain. He also narrated it in another place in Tafsir, and Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah narrated it from several routes from Shu'bah with this chain.[^11] Al-Waqidi narrated it from Muhammad ibn Mu'adh al-Ansari, from Khubayb ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, from Hafs ibn 'Asim, from Abu Sa'id ibn al-Mu'alla, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, and mentioned something similar.

There occurs in the Muwatta' of the Imam Malik ibn Anas something that deserves to be pointed out, for he narrated it from al-'Ala' ibn 'Abd

Commentary of Ibn Kathir (Tafsir al-Quran al-'Azim) on surah 1, verse 1 (part 2 of 5):

al-Rahman ibn Ya'qub al-Huraqi: that Abu Sa'id, the mawla (freed client) of 'Amir ibn Kurayz, informed them that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called out to Ubayy ibn Ka'b while he was praying in the mosque. When he finished his prayer, he came up to him. He said: The Prophet (ﷺ) placed his hand on my hand, while he wanted to leave through the door of the mosque. Then he said: "I truly hope that you will not leave through the door of the mosque until you learn a surah the like of which has not been sent down in the Torah, nor in the Gospel, nor in the Furqan (the Qur'an)." Ubayy said: So I began to slow my walk in hope of that. Then I said: "O Messenger of Allah, what is the surah you promised me?" He said: "How do you recite when you begin the prayer?" He said: So I recited to him: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ until I reached its end. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "It is this surah, and it is the seven oft-repeated (al-sab' al-mathani) and the great Qur'an which I have been given."

[Muwatta' (1/83).]

As for this Abu Sa'id, he is not Abu Sa'id ibn al-Mu'alla, as Ibn al-Athir held in Jami' al-Usul and those who followed him. Ibn al-Mu'alla was a Companion from the Ansar, whereas this one is a Tabi'i (Successor) from the mawali of Khuza'ah. That hadith is connected (muttasil) and sound, while this one apparently is disconnected (munqati'), if Abu Sa'id did not hear it from Ubayy ibn Ka'b. If he did hear it from him, then it meets the conditions of Muslim. And Allah knows best. Moreover, it has been narrated from Ubayy ibn Ka'b through more than one channel, as the Imam Ahmad said:

 'Affan narrated to us: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Ibrahim narrated to us: al-'Ala' ibn 'Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, from his father, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out to Ubayy ibn Ka'b while he was praying, and said: "O Ubayy!" He turned but did not answer him. Then he (Ubayy) said: Ubayy, make it brief. Then he turned to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "Peace be upon you, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "And upon you be peace. What prevented you, O Ubayy, from answering me when I called you?" He said: O Messenger of Allah, I was in prayer. He said: "Do you not find in what Allah revealed to me: ﴿Respond to Allah and to the Messenger when he calls you to that which gives you life﴾ [al-Anfal: 24]?" He said: Yes, O Messenger of Allah. I will not do it again. He said: "Would you like me to teach you a surah that has not been sent down in the Torah, nor in the Gospel, nor in the Psalms, nor in the Furqan (the Qur'an), the like of which does not exist?" I said: Yes, O Messenger of Allah. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I truly hope that I will not leave this door until you learn it." He said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took my hand and talked with me, and I was slow, fearing that he would reach the door before he finished the discourse. When we came near the door, I said: O Messenger of Allah, what is the surah you promised me? He said: "What do you recite in the prayer?" He said: So I recited to him Umm al-Qur'an (the Mother of the Qur'an). He said: "By Him in whose hand my soul is, nothing like it has been sent down in the Torah, nor in the Gospel, nor in the Psalms, nor in the Furqan. Indeed it is the seven oft-repeated."

Al-Tirmidhi narrated it from Qutaybah, from al-Darawardi, from al-'Ala', from his father, from Abu Hurayrah, and mentioned it [similarly]. In his version: "Indeed it is among the seven oft-repeated and the great Qur'an which I have been given." Then he said: This is a hasan sahih (good and sound) hadith.

Also on this topic, from Anas ibn Malik. 'Abd Allah ibn [al-Imam] Ahmad narrated it from Isma'il ibn Abi Ma'mar, from Abu Usamah, from 'Abd al-Hamid ibn Ja'far, from al-'Ala', from his father, from Abu Hurayrah, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, and mentioned it at length, in similar or close wording. Al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i both narrated it from Abu 'Ammar Husayn ibn Hurayth, from al-Fadl ibn Musa, from 'Abd al-Hamid ibn Ja'far, from al-'Ala', from his father, from Abu Hurayrah, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Nothing like Umm al-Qur'an has been sent down in the Torah or the Gospel. It is the seven oft-repeated, and it is divided between Me and My servant." This is the wording of al-Nasa'i. Al-Tirmidhi said: hasan gharib (good and unusual).

Imam Ahmad said: Muhammad ibn 'Ubayd narrated to us: Hashim, meaning Ibn al-Bariyd, narrated to us: 'Abd Allah ibn Muhammad ibn 'Aqil narrated to us, from Ibn Ja'bir, who said: I came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he had poured out water (for ablution). I said: Peace be upon you, O Messenger of Allah. He did not return my greeting. He said: I said again: Peace be upon you, O Messenger of Allah. He did not return it to me. He said: I said again: Peace be upon you, O Messenger of Allah. He did not return it to me. He said: So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) walked away, and I was behind him, until he entered his dwelling, and I entered the mosque and sat, dejected and sad. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came out to me, having purified himself, and said: "Upon you be peace and the mercy of Allah. And upon you be peace and the mercy of Allah. And upon you be peace and the mercy of Allah." Then he said: "Shall I not inform you, O 'Abd Allah ibn Jabir, of the best surah in the Qur'an?" I said: Yes, O Messenger of Allah. He said: "Recite: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ until you finish it."

[Musnad (4/177).] This is a good chain (isnad). Ibn 'Aqil is relied upon by the great imams. This 'Abd Allah ibn Jabir is the Companion; Ibn al-Jawzi mentioned that he is al-'Abdi, and Allah knows best. It is also said that he is 'Abd Allah ibn Jabir al-Ansari al-Bayadi, as mentioned by the hafiz Ibn 'Asakir [and this is what the hafiz Ibn Hajar preferred in his book Ta'jil al-Manfa'ah (p. 145)].

By this hadith and similar ones, some scholars have argued for the superiority of certain verses and surahs over others, as is reported from many scholars, among them Ishaq ibn Rahawayh, Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi, and Ibn al-Hisar from the Malikis. Another group held that there is no superiority in this matter, because the whole is the speech of Allah, and so that the notion of superiority does not imply a deficiency in what is deemed less excellent. Even though all are excellent, al-Qurtubi transmitted this from al-Ash'ari, Abu Bakr al-Baqillani, Abu Hatim ibn Hibban al-Busti, Yahya ibn Yahya, and a report from Imam Malik [as well].

Another hadith: al-Bukhari said in Fada'il al-Qur'an: Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us: Wahb narrated to us: Hisham narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Ma'bad, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: We were on a journey of ours, and we halted, and a slave girl came and said: The chief of the tribe has been stung by a scorpion, and our men are absent. Is there anyone among you who can perform ruqyah (healing recitation)? A man got up with her, whom we did not know to be practicing ruqyah. He recited over him, and he recovered. He ordered that he be given thirty sheep, and he gave us milk to drink. When he returned, we said to him: Did you know ruqyah well, or were you reciting it? He said: No, I only recited with Umm al-Kitab. We said: Do not speak of anything until we come to, or ask, the Prophet (ﷺ). When we arrived in Madinah, we mentioned it to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: "And how did he know it was a ruqyah? Divide [the sheep] and set aside a share for me."

Abu Ma'mar said: 'Abd al-Warith narrated to us: Hisham narrated to us: Muhammad ibn Sirin narrated to us: Ma'bad ibn Sirin narrated to me, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, with this [hadith].

Thus Muslim and Abu Dawud narrated it through Hisham, who is Ibn Hassan, from Ibn Sirin, with it. In some narrations of Muslim for this hadith: that Abu Sa'id was the one who performed ruqyah over that sting victim (saline, meaning the one who is stung, called so out of optimism).

Another hadith: Muslim in his Sahih, and al-Nasa'i in his Sunan, narrated from the hadith of Abu al-Ahwas Sallam ibn Sulaym, from 'Ammar ibn Ruzayq, from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Isa ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: While the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was with him was Jibril, he heard a creaking above him. Jibril raised his gaze to the sky and said: This is a gate that has been opened from the sky, which has never been opened before. He said: Then an angel descended from it and came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "Rejoice in two lights which you have been given, which no prophet before you was given: the Opening of the Book (al-Fatihah) and the closing verses of Surat al-Baqarah. You will not recite a letter of either of them except that you will be given it." This is the wording of al-Nasa'i.

Muslim has a similar hadith also: Muslim said: Ishaq ibn Ibrahim al-Hanzali narrated to us, that is Ibn Rahawayh, narrated to us: Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah narrated to us, from al-'Ala', meaning Ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Ya'qub al-Huraqi, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Whoever prays a prayer in which he does not recite Umm al-Qur'an, it is khidaj (deficient), three times, incomplete." It was said to Abu Hurayrah: Indeed we are sometimes behind the imam. He said: Recite it to yourself, for I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: I have divided the prayer between Me and My servant into two halves, and to My servant is what he asks. When the servant says: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Fatihah: 2], Allah says: My servant has praised Me. When he says: ﴿The Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾ [al-Fatihah: 3], Allah says: My servant has extolled Me. When he says: ﴿Master of the Day of Judgment﴾ [al-Fatihah: 4], Allah says: My servant has glorified Me." And once he said: "My servant has entrusted to Me. When he says: ﴿It is You we worship and You we ask for help﴾ [al-Fatihah: 5], He says: This is between Me and My servant, and to My servant is what he asks. When he says: ﴿Guide us to the straight path, the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favor, not of those who have evoked [Your] anger or of those who are astray﴾ [al-Fatihah: 6-7], He says: This is for My servant, and to My servant is what he asks."

Al-Nasa'i narrated it likewise from Ishaq ibn Rahawayh. [Sahih Muslim (395) and Sunan al-Nasa'i al-Kubra (8013).] Both of them also narrated it from Qutaybah, from Malik, from al-'Ala', from Abu al-Sa'ib, mawla of Hisham ibn Zuhrah, from Abu Hurayrah, with it. In this version: "So half of it is for Me and half of it is for My servant, and to My servant is what he asks."

Ibn Ishaq also narrated it likewise from al-'Ala'. Muslim narrated it from the hadith of Ibn Juraij, from al-'Ala', from Abu al-Sa'ib in this manner.

He also narrated it from the hadith of Ibn Abi Uways, from al-'Ala', from his father and Abu al-Sa'ib, both from Abu Hurayrah.

Al-Tirmidhi said: This is a hasan hadith. I asked Abu Zur'ah about it, and he said: Both hadiths are sahih; the one who says "from al-'Ala', from his father," and the one who says "from al-'Ala', from Abu al-Sa'ib."

'Abd Allah, the son of Imam Ahmad, narrated this hadith from the hadith of al-'Ala', from his father, from Abu Hurayrah, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, at length.

Ibn Jarir said: Salih ibn Mismar al-Marwazi narrated to us, saying: Zayd ibn al-Hubab narrated to us, saying: 'Anbasa ibn Sa'id narrated to us, from Mutarrif ibn Tarif, from Sa'id ibn Ishaq ibn Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah, from Jabir ibn 'Abdullah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah the Exalted says: I have divided the prayer between Myself and My servant into two halves, and he shall have what he asks. When the servant says: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾, He says: My servant has praised Me. When he says: ﴿The Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾, He says: My servant has extolled Me. Then He says: This is between Me and My servant, and he shall have what remains."

Ibn Kathir: This is gharib (singular) from this route.

Then, the discussion of matters related to this hadith that pertain specifically to al-Fatihah, from several aspects:

The first: the word "prayer" (salah) is used in it while the intended meaning is recitation, as in His saying: ﴿And do not recite your prayer aloud or silently, but seek a way between that﴾ [al-Isra' 110], meaning: your recitation, as is explicitly stated in the Sahih from Ibn 'Abbas [Sahih al-Bukhari no. 7490 and Sahih Muslim no. 446]. Likewise He said in this hadith: "I have divided the prayer between Myself and My servant into two halves, so half of it is for Me and half of it is for My servant, and My servant shall have what he asks." Then He explained the details of this division in the recitation of al-Fatihah, which indicates the greatness of recitation in the prayer and that it is among its greatest pillars, since worship was used in a general sense while only one part of it, which is recitation, was intended; just as the word recitation was used while prayer was intended, in His saying: ﴿And the recitation of dawn; indeed, the recitation of dawn is ever witnessed﴾ [al-Isra' 78], meaning the Fajr prayer, as is explicitly stated in the Two Sahihs, that the angels of the night and the angels of the day witness it. All of this indicates that recitation is necessary in the prayer, and this is a consensus of the scholars.

However, they differed on a question which we mention in the second aspect: whether al-Fatihah is specifically required for recitation in the prayer, or whether it or something else suffices. There are two well-known opinions. According to Abu Hanifah and those who agreed with him among his companions and others, it is not specifically required; rather, whatever Qur'an one recites suffices in the prayer. They argued from the generality of His saying: ﴿So recite what is easy of the Qur'an﴾ [al-Muzzammil 20], and from what is established in the Two Sahihs, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah concerning the one who prayed badly, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: "When you stand for the prayer, say takbir, then recite what is easy for you of the Qur'an." They said: He commanded him to recite what is easy and did not specify al-Fatihah or anything else, which indicates what we have said.

The second opinion: recitation of al-Fatihah is specifically required in the prayer, and the prayer is not valid without it. This is the view of the remaining imams: Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad ibn Hanbal and their companions, and the majority of scholars. They argued for this by this hadith mentioned, where the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, said: "Whoever prays a prayer in which he does not recite Umm al-Qur'an (al-Fatihah), it is khidaj." Khidaj means deficient, as it was explained in the hadith: "incomplete." They also argued by what is established in the Two Sahihs from the hadith of al-Zuhri, from Mahmud ibn al-Rabi', from 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is no prayer for one who does not recite the Opening of the Book (al-Fatihah)" [Sahih al-Bukhari no. 756 and Sahih Muslim no. 394]. In Sahih Ibn Khuzaymah and Sahih Ibn Hibban, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A prayer in which Umm al-Qur'an is not recited is not valid" [Sahih Ibn Khuzaymah no. 490 and Sahih Ibn Hibban no. 459, Mawarid]. The hadiths on this subject are many, and the detailed debate here would be lengthy; we have pointed to their evidence, may Allah have mercy on them.

Then, the position of al-Shafi'i and a group of scholars is that it is obligatory to recite it in every rak'ah. Others said: it is obligatory only in most of the rak'ahs. Al-Hasan and most of the Basrans said: it is obligatory only in one rak'ah of the prayers, taking by the absolute wording of the hadith: "There is no prayer for one who does not recite the Opening of the Book."

Abu Hanifah, his companions, al-Thawri and al-Awza'i said: its recitation is not specifically required; rather, if one recites something other than it, it suffices, due to His saying: ﴿So recite what is easy of the Qur'an﴾ [al-Muzzammil 20], [as previously mentioned]. And Allah knows best.

Ibn Majah narrated from the hadith of Abu Sufyan al-Sa'di, from Abu Nadrah, from Abu Sa'id, traced to the Prophet: "There is no prayer for one who does not recite in every rak'ah the Hamd and a surah, in an obligatory prayer or otherwise" [Sunan Ibn Majah no. 839. al-Busiri said in al-Zawa'id (1/291): "This chain is weak; Abu Sufyan al-Sa'di, whose name is Tarif ibn Shihab, and it is said Ibn Sa'd, Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: they agreed on his weakness." But Abu Sufyan has been corroborated: Qatadah narrated it from Abu Nadrah, from Abu Sa'id, traced to the Prophet, with the wording: "We were commanded to recite the Opening of the Book and what is easy," narrated by Abu Dawud in his Sunan no. 818]. There is room for scrutiny regarding its authenticity, and the clarification of all this is in the large book on rulings, and Allah knows best.

The third aspect: is it obligatory for the follower (ma'mum) to recite al-Fatihah? There are three opinions among the scholars:

The first: it is obligatory upon him to recite it, just as it is obligatory upon his imam, due to the generality of the hadiths mentioned earlier.

The second: the follower is not obliged to recite anything at all, neither al-Fatihah nor anything else, whether in the audible or silent prayer, based on what Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal narrated in his Musnad, from Jabir ibn 'Abdullah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Whoever has an imam, the imam's recitation is his recitation." However, its chain contains weakness [narrated by Ahmad in al-Musnad (3/339); Imam al-Zayla'i extensively discussed the routes of this hadith in his book Nasb al-Rayah (2/6-14), which suffices from mentioning it here]. Malik narrated it from Wahb ibn Kaysan, from Jabir, as his own statement [narrated by al-Bayhaqi in al-Sunan al-Kubra (2/160) through the route of Malik, and he said: "This is the correct statement from Jabir, as his own words, not raised (marfu')."] Many routes of this hadith have been related, but none of them is authentically from the Prophet (ﷺ), and Allah knows best.

The third opinion: recitation is obligatory upon the follower in the silent prayer, as previously mentioned, but it is not obligatory in the audible prayer, based on what is established in Sahih Muslim from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The imam is appointed only to be followed; so when he says takbir, say takbir, and when he recites, be silent," and he mentioned the rest of the hadith [Sahih Muslim no. 404].

Likewise, the compilers of the Sunan narrated it: Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "And when he recites, be silent" [Sunan Abi Dawud no. 604; Sunan al-Nasa'i (2/141, 142); Sunan Ibn Majah no. 846. Abu Dawud said: "This addition, 'and when he recites, be silent,' is not preserved; the error is from Abu Khalid in our view." Muslim authenticated this addition in his Sahih, and al-Daraqutni criticized it in al-Tatabbu' (p. 239). See the response of Abu Mas'ud al-Dimashqi in the margins of al-Tatabbu'; Shaykh Nasir al-Din al-Albani also has a discussion on this addition in al-Irwa' (2/121), and he judged it hasan]. Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj also authenticated it, so these two hadiths indicate the soundness of this opinion, which is an older view of al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, and a narration from Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal.

The purpose of mentioning these issues here is to explain that Surah al-Fatihah is specified with rulings that do not apply to other surahs, and Allah knows best.

Al-Hafiz Abu Bakr al-Bazzar said: Ibrahim ibn Sa'id al-Jawhari narrated to us, saying: Ghassan ibn 'Ubayd narrated to us, from Abu 'Imran al-Jawni, from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When you lay your side on the bedding and recite the Opening of the Book and ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾, you are safe from everything except death" [Musnad al-Bazzar no. 3109, Kashf al-Astar; in its chain is Ghassan ibn 'Ubayd, of whom Ibn 'Adi said: "The weakness in his narrations is evident."]

The discussion on the explanation of seeking refuge (al-isti'adhah). Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Take what is forgiving, enjoin what is good, and turn away from the ignorant. And if an evil suggestion from Satan should tempt you, then seek refuge in Allah; indeed, He is Hearing and Knowing﴾ [al-A'raf 199-200]. He also says: ﴿Repel evil with that which is better; We are most knowing of what they describe. And say: My Lord, I seek refuge in You from the incitements of the devils. And I seek refuge in You, my Lord, lest they be present with me﴾ [al-Mu'minun 96-98]. And He says: ﴿Repel with that which is better, and then the one between whom and you is enmity will become as though he were a devoted friend. But none is granted it except those who are patient, and none is granted it except one of great fortune. And if an evil suggestion from Satan should tempt you, then seek refuge in Allah; indeed, He is the Hearing, the Knowing﴾ [Fussilat 34-36].

These are three verses with no fourth in their meaning, namely that Allah commands dealing kindly with the human enemy and doing good to him, so that his good nature may turn him back to friendship and amity, and He commands seeking refuge in Him from the Satanic enemy without fail, since he accepts neither conciliation nor kindness and seeks nothing but the ruin of the son of Adam, because of the intense enmity between him and our father Adam from before; as He said: ﴿O children of Adam, do not let Satan tempt you as he removed your parents from Paradise﴾ [al-A'raf 27], and He said: ﴿Indeed, Satan is an enemy to you, so take him as an enemy. He only invites his party that they may be among the companions of the Blaze﴾ [Fatir 6], and He said: ﴿Then do you take him and his descendants as allies instead of Me while they are an enemy to you? Wretched is the exchange for the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Kahf 50]. He swore to Adam, "Indeed, I am to you of the sincere advisers," and he lied. So how would be his dealing with us, when he said: ﴿By Your might, I will surely mislead them all, except Your sincere servants among them﴾ [Sad 82-83]? He also said: ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Indeed, he has no authority over those who believe and rely upon their Lord﴾ [al-Nahl 98-99].

A group of reciters and others said: we seek refuge after the recitation, relying on the apparent context of the verse, and to repel self-admiration after finishing the worship. Among those who held this view was Hamzah, as transmitted by Ibn Qulawayh from him, and Abu Hatim al-Sijistani. Abu al-Qasim Yusuf ibn 'Ali ibn Jubara al-Hudhali al-Maghribi related this in his book al-Kamil.

It is also narrated from Abu Hurayrah, and it is gharib.

[Fakhr al-Din Muhammad ibn Umar al-Razi also reported it in his tafsir, from Ibn Sirin in one narration, and he said: "This is the view of Ibrahim al-Nakha'i and Dawud ibn Ali al-Isfahani al-Zahiri." Al-Qurtubi relayed from Abu Bakr ibn al-Arabi, from al-Majmu'ah, from Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, that the reciter seeks refuge after al-Fatihah. Ibn al-Arabi considered this strange. A third view was also reported, namely seeking refuge both at the beginning and at the end, combining the two proofs. Fakhr al-Din reported this.] [[Tafsir al-Qurtubi (1/88).]]

The well-known view, held by the majority, is that seeking refuge (al-istiʿadhah) to repel the whispering (al-waswas) during it is only before recitation. According to them, the meaning of the verse is: ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan﴾ [al-Nahl: 98], that is, when you intend to recite, as in His saying: ﴿When you rise to prayer, wash your faces and your hands﴾ and so on [al-Ma'idah: 6], that is, when you intend to stand. The evidence for this is the hadiths from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to that effect. Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn Ātash [in all the manuscripts and the Musnad it reads "Anas", and the correct reading is what we have adopted] narrated to us: Ja'far ibn Sulayman narrated to us, from Ali ibn Ali al-Rifa'i al-Yashkuri, from Abu al-Mutawakkil al-Naji, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ rose at night to pray, he began his prayer and said takbir, then said: "Subhanaka Allahumma wa bihamdika, wa tabaraka ismuka, wa ta'ala jadduka, wa la ilaha ghayruka" [Glory be to You, O Allah, and praise be to You; blessed is Your name, exalted is Your majesty, and there is no god other than You]. And he would say: "La ilaha illa Allah" three times, then say: "A'udhu billahi as-Sami' al-'Alim, min ash-shaytan ar-rajim, min hamzihi wa nafkhihi wa nafthihi" [I seek refuge in Allah, the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing, from the accursed Satan, from his whispering, his blowing and his spitting].

The people of the Four Sunan also narrated it through Ja'far ibn Sulayman, from Ali ibn Ali, who is al-Rifa'i. [The Musnad (3/50), Sunan Abi Dawud no. (775), Sunan al-Tirmidhi no. (242), Sunan al-Nasa'i (2/132), Sunan Ibn Majah no. (804).] Al-Tirmidhi said: "It is the most famous hadith on this subject." They explained "hamz" as madness (al-mawtah), which is strangling, "nafkh" as pride, and "nafth" as poetry.

Abu Dawud and Ibn Majah also narrated it from the hadith of Shu'bah, from Amr ibn Murrah, from Asim al-'Anazi, from Nafi' ibn Jubayr ibn Mut'im, from his father, who said: I saw the Messenger of Allah ﷺ when he began the prayer, and he said: "Allahu akbar kabiran" three times, "al-hamdu lillahi kathiran" three times, "subhan Allahi bukratan wa asila" three times, "Allahumma inni a'udhu bika mina ash-shaytan, min hamzihi wa nafkhihi wa nafthihi."
[Amr said: his hamz is madness, his nafkh is pride, and his nafth is poetry.] [Sunan Abi Dawud no. (764), Sunan Ibn Majah no. (807). Ibn Hibban narrated it in his Sahih no. (443) through the chain of Shu'bah.]

Ibn Majah said: Ali ibn al-Mundhir narrated to us, Ibn Fudayl narrated to us, Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib narrated to us, from Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, from Ibn Mas'ud, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "Allahumma inni a'udhu bika mina ash-shaytan ar-rajim, wa hamzihi wa nafkhihi wa nafthihi."
He said: his hamz is madness, his nafth is poetry, and his nafkh is pride. [Sunan Ibn Majah no. (808). Ibn Khuzaymah narrated it in his Sahih no. (472) through Muhammad ibn Fudayl. Al-Busiri said in al-Zawa'id (1/285): "This chain is weak; Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib became confused in his later years, and Muhammad ibn Fudayl heard from him after the confusion."]

Imam Ahmad said: Ishaq ibn Yusuf narrated to us, Sharik narrated to us, from Ya'la ibn Ata', from a man who narrated to him that he heard Abu Umamah al-Bahili say: When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ rose to prayer, he said takbir three times, then said: "La ilaha illa Allah" three times, and "Subhan Allahi wa bihamdihi" three times. Then he said: "A'udhu billahi min ash-shaytan ar-rajim, min hamzihi wa nafkhihi wa nafthihi." [Al-Musnad (5/253).]

The hafiz Abu Ya'la Ahmad ibn Ali ibn al-Muthanna al-Mawsili said in his Musnad: Abdullah ibn Umar ibn Aban al-Kufi narrated to us, Ali ibn Hisham ibn al-Barid narrated to us, from Yazid ibn Ziyad, from Abd al-Malik ibn Umayr, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: Two men quarrelled in the presence of the Prophet ﷺ, and one of them's nose swelled from anger. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Indeed I know a word which, if he said it, what he feels would leave him: A'udhu billahi min ash-shaytan ar-rajim."

Al-Nasa'i also narrated it in al-Yawm wa al-Layla, from Yusuf ibn Isa al-Marwazi, from al-Fadl ibn Musa, from Yazid ibn Ziyad ibn Abi al-Ja'd, with the same chain. [Sunan al-Nasa'i al-Kubra no. (10223).] [In a manuscript: "al-Ja'diyyah".]

This hadith was also narrated by Ahmad ibn Hanbal from Abu Sa'id, from Za'idah; by Abu Dawud from Yusuf ibn Musa, from Jarir ibn Abd al-Hamid; and by al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i in al-Yawm wa al-Layla from Bundar, from Ibn Mahdi, from al-Thawri; and al-Nasa'i also from the hadith of Za'idah ibn Qudamah. All three [Yazid, Za'idah, and Jarir] narrated from Abd al-Malik ibn Umayr, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla, from Mu'adh ibn Jabal, who said: Two men cursed each other in the presence of the Prophet ﷺ, and one of them became extremely angry, so that it seemed to me that his nose was swelling from the intensity of his anger. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed I know a word which, if he said it, what he feels of anger would leave him." He said: "What is it, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "He says: Allahumma inni a'udhu bika min ash-shaytan ar-rajim." He said: Mu'adh began to order him to say it, but he refused [wa mahak (and woe to you)] and his anger kept increasing. This is the wording of Abu Dawud. [Al-Musnad (5/244), Sunan Abi Dawud no. (4780), Sunan al-Tirmidhi no. (3452), Sunan al-Nasa'i al-Kubra nos. (10221, 10222).] [The bracketed words are from ج، ب، and Abu Dawud; in أ it reads "wa mahal".]

Al-Tirmidhi said: It is mursal, meaning that Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla did not meet Mu'adh ibn Jabal, for he died before the year twenty [AH].

I say: Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla may have heard it from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, as mentioned earlier, and conveyed it from Mu'adh ibn Jabal, since this incident was witnessed by more than one of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them.

Al-Bukhari said: Uthman ibn Abi Shaybah narrated to us, Jarir narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from Adi ibn Thabit, who said: Sulayman ibn Surad said: Two men cursed each other in the presence of the Prophet ﷺ while we were sitting with him. One of them was cursing his companion in anger, his face reddened. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed I know a word which, if he said it, what he feels would leave him: if he said, 'A'udhu billahi min ash-shaytan ar-rajim.'" They said to the man: "Do you not hear what the Messenger of Allah ﷺ says?" He said: "I am not mad." [Sahih al-Bukhari no. (6115).]

It was also narrated with Muslim, Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i, through various routes, from al-A'mash, with the same wording. [Sahih Muslim no. (2610), Sunan Abi Dawud no. (4781), Sunan al-Nasa'i al-Kubra nos. (10224, 10225).]

Many hadiths about seeking refuge have come down, too many to mention here; their proper place is the books of adhkar (remembrances) and fada'il al-a'mal (virtues of deeds). And Allah knows best. It has been narrated that when the Qur'an was first revealed to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, Jibril, upon him peace, commanded him to seek refuge, as Imam Abu Ja'far ibn Jarir said:

Abu Kurayb narrated to us, Uthman ibn Sa'id narrated to us, Bishr ibn Imarah narrated to us, Abu Rawq narrated to us, from al-Dahhak, from Abdullah ibn Abbas, who said: The first thing Jibril said when he came down to Muhammad ﷺ was: "O Muhammad, seek refuge." He said: "I seek refuge in Allah, the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing, from the accursed Satan." Then he said: "Say: Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim." Then he said: ﴿Read in the name of your Lord who created﴾. Abdullah said: This is the first surah Allah revealed to Muhammad ﷺ, in the tongue of Jibril. [Tafsir al-Tabari (1/113).] This report is gharib (strange), and I have mentioned it only so that it may be known, for its chain contains weakness and a break. And Allah knows best.

Issue: The majority of scholars hold that seeking refuge is recommended (mustahabb), not obligatory (mutahattim) such that one who abandons it sins. Fakhr al-Din reported that Ata' ibn Abi Rabah held it to be obligatory in prayer and outside it, whenever one intends to recite. Ibn Sirin said: If one seeks refuge once in one's lifetime, that suffices to discharge the obligation. Fakhr al-Din supported Ata's view with the apparent meaning of the verse, ﴿So seek refuge﴾, which is a command whose apparent sense is obligation; with the Prophet ﷺ's constant practice of it; and because it repels the evil of Satan, and whatever a obligation cannot be completed without is itself obligatory; and because seeking refuge is more cautious, which is one of the methods of establishing obligation. Some said it was obligatory on the Prophet ﷺ alone, not on his community. It is reported from Malik that he did not seek refuge in obligatory prayers, but did seek it on the first night of the Ramadan night prayers (qiyam).

Issue: Al-Shafi'i said in al-Imla': one should say it aloud, but if one says it quietly there is no harm. In al-Umm he said it is optional, since Ibn Umar said it quietly and Abu Hurayrah said it aloud. Al-Shafi'i's view differed regarding the rest of the rak'ahs other than the first: is seeking refuge recommended in them? There are two opinions, and he preferred that it is not recommended. And Allah knows best. If the one seeking refuge says "A'udhu billahi min ash-shaytan ar-rajim," this suffices according to al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifah. Some added: "A'udhu billahi as-Sami' al-'Alim." Others said: one should say "A'udhu billahi min ash-shaytan ar-rajim, inna Allaha huwa as-Sami' al-'Alim." This was said by al-Thawri and al-Awza'i. It is reported from some that one says "A'stʿidhu billahi min ash-shaytan ar-rajim" to match the wording of the verse and the hadith of al-Dahhak from Ibn Abbas mentioned above. But the authentic hadiths, as previously cited, are more deserving of being followed than this. And Allah knows best.

Issue: Seeking refuge in prayer is only for recitation, according to Abu Hanifah and Muhammad. Abu Yusuf said: rather, it is for prayer [in general]. On this view, the follower (al-ma'mum) seeks refuge even though he does not recite. In the Eid prayer, one seeks refuge after the opening takbir and before the Eid takbirat; the majority say it is after them and before the recitation.

Among the subtleties of seeking refuge is that it purifies the mouth from the idle talk and obscenity it used to engage in, perfumes it, and prepares it for reciting the speech of Allah. It is also seeking help from Allah, acknowledging His power and the servant's weakness and inability to resist this manifest and hidden enemy, whom none can restrain or repel except Allah, who created him. He accepts no appeasement and cannot be placated with kindness, unlike the enemy from among mankind, as the verses of the Qur'an in three of the oft-repeated (al-mathani) surahs indicate. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them, and sufficient is your Lord as Disposer of affairs﴾ [al-Isra': 65]. The angels descended to fight the human enemy on the day of Badr. Whoever is killed by the human enemy is a martyr; whoever is killed by the hidden enemy is cast out; whoever is overcome by the outward enemy is rewarded; whoever is subdued by the inward enemy is afflicted or sinful. Since Satan sees the human being from where he cannot see him, the human seeks refuge from him in the One who sees him while he does not see Him.

Section: Al-isti'adhah (seeking refuge) is taking refuge with Allah and clinging to His threshold from the evil of every evil-doer. Al-i'adhah is for repelling harm, while al-liyadh is for seeking the acquisition of good, as al-Mutanabbi said:

O You to whom I cling for what I hope for,
and in whom I seek refuge from what I fear.

**Section: The meaning of seeking refuge (al-istiʿadha)**

Our text of the poem (from the first line of the passage above) is by al-Mutanabbi:

*"People cannot mend a bone that you have broken, / and they cannot break a bone that you have mended."*

Ibn Kathir cites these two lines in *al-Bidaya wa'l-Nihaya* (11/275) and says: "It has reached me that our shaykh, the scholar Shaykh al-Islam Ahmad ibn Taymiyya (may Allah have mercy on him), used to object to al-Mutanabbi's exaggeration about a created being, and would say: 'This is only fitting for the presence of Allah, glorified and exalted be He.' And the scholar Shams al-Din Ibn al-Qayyim (may Allah have mercy on him) told me that he heard the aforementioned Shaykh Taqi al-Din say: 'I have sometimes recited these two lines in prostration, asking Allah by what they contain of humility and submission.'"

The meaning of *aʿudhu billahi min al-shaytan al-rajim* ("I seek refuge in Allah from Satan, the accursed"): that is, I seek the protection of the presence of Allah from Satan (al-shaytan, the devil, the arch-adversary of humankind), lest he harm me in my religion or my worldly life, or keep me from doing what I have been commanded, or incite me to do what I have been forbidden. For indeed, Satan is not restrained from a person except by Allah. For this reason, Allah, exalted is He, commanded that one should placate and deal gently with the human devil (*shaytan al-ins*) by showing him kindness, so that his own nature might turn him back from the harm he is inflicting. And He commanded seeking refuge in Allah from the devil of the jinn, because he does not accept a bribe, and kindness does not affect him, for he is evil by nature, and only the One who created him can restrain him from you.

This meaning appears in three verses of the Qur'an, and I know of no fourth. The first is His saying in Surat al-Aʿraf: ﴿Take what is easy, enjoin what is right, and turn away from the ignorant.﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 199]. This concerns dealing with enemies among humankind. Then He said: ﴿And if an evil prompting from Satan should stir you, then seek refuge in Allah. Indeed, He is Hearing and Knowing.﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 200]. The Exalted also said in Surat "Qad Aflaha al-Mu'minun": ﴿Repel evil with that which is better; We are most knowing of what they describe. And say, "My Lord, I seek refuge in You from the proddings of the devils. And I seek refuge in You, my Lord, lest they be present with me."﴾ [al-Muʾminun: 96–98]. And He said in Surat "Ha Mim al-Sajdah": ﴿And not equal are the good deed and the bad. Repel evil with that which is better, and thereupon the one between whom and you there is enmity will become as though he were a devoted friend. But none is granted it except those who are patient, and none is granted it except one of great fortune. And if an evil prompting from Satan should stir you, then seek refuge in Allah. Indeed, He is the Hearing, the Knowing.﴾ [Fussilat: 34–36].

The word *al-shaytan* in the Arabic language is derived from *shatana*, meaning "to be far away." He is far away by his nature from the natures of humankind, and far away by his wickedness from every good. It has also been said that it derives from *shaana* (to be hostile or to be abhorrent), because he was created from fire. Some say that both meanings are correct, but the first is more correct, and the usage of the Arabs points to it. Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt said, describing what was given to Sulayman (peace be upon him):

*"Whatever rebellious devil (shatin) disobeys him, he [Sulayman] restrains him, / then he is cast into prison and chains."*

He said "shatin" and did not say "shaʾit."

Al-Nabigha al-Dhubyani, whose name is Ziyad ibn ʿAmr ibn Muʿawiya ibn Jabir ibn Dabab ibn Yarbuʿ ibn Murra ibn Saʿd ibn Dhubyan, said:

*"Far away from you, with Suʿad, is a distant (shatun) journey, / so she departed, while the heart was held captive by her."*

That is, a distant road separated her from him.

[Sibawayh said: The Arabs say, "Fulan tashaytana" (so-and-so acted like a devil) when he does the deed of a devil; and if it were from *shaʾa*, they would say *tashayyaʾa*.] And *al-shaytan*, according to the correct view, is derived from distance. For this reason they call every rebellious one among the jinn, humankind, or animals a devil. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And thus We have made for every prophet an enemy: devils from among mankind and jinn, inspiring to one another decorative speech as deception.﴾ [al-Anʿam: 112].

In *Musnad* Imam Ahmad, from Abu Dhar (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "O Abu Dhar, seek refuge in Allah from the devils of humankind and jinn." I said: "Are there devils among mankind?" He said: "Yes."

In *Sahih Muslim*, from Abu Dhar also, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Prayer is cut off by a woman, a donkey, and a black dog." I said: "O Messenger of Allah, what is it about the black dog rather than the red or the yellow?" He said: "The black dog is a devil." [Narrated by al-Tabari in his *Tafsir* (1/111).]

And Ibn Wahb said: Hisham ibn Saʿd informed me, from Zayd ibn Aslam, from his father, that ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) mounted a horse, and it began to strut, and he did not strike it, and it only increased in strutting. So he dismounted and said: "You have carried me only upon a devil! I did not dismount from it until I disowned myself." Its chain of narration is sound. [Narrated by al-Tabari in his *Tafsir* (1/111).]

*Al-rajim* is on the pattern *faʿil* in the sense of *maf'ul* (the passive), meaning that he is stoned (*marjum*), driven away (*matrud*) from all good, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We have certainly adorned the nearest heaven with lamps and made them missiles against the devils.﴾ [al-Mulk: 5]. And Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, We have decorated the nearest heaven with an adornment of stars, and as protection from every rebellious devil. They cannot listen to the Exalted Assembly, and they are pelted from every side, repelled, and for them is a perpetual punishment. Except one who snatches a fragment, and he is pursued by a piercing flame.﴾ [al-Saffat: 6–10]. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We have certainly placed within the sky constellations and adorned it for the observers. And We have protected it from every accursed devil. Except one who steals a hearing, and he is pursued by a clear flame.﴾ [al-Hijr: 16–18], and other verses besides these.

[It has also been said that *rajim* means *rajim* (one who stones), because he stones people with whisperings and evil thoughts; but the first (meaning) is more well-known.]

[[The author's speech has been abridged because of its great length.]]

The seven canonical readers (al-qurra' al-sab'ah) read the *dal* of His words ﴿al-hamdu lillah﴾ with a *damma*, and it is a subject and predicate (mubtada' and khabar). It is also reported from Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah and Ru'bah ibn al-'Ajjaj that they recited "al-hamda lillah" with a *fatha*, which is governed by an implied verb (idmar fi'l). Ibn Abi 'Ablah read "al-hamdu lullah" with a *damma* on the *dal* and the *lam*, assimilating the second vowel to the first. It has supporting parallels, but it is *shadh* (irregular). It is also reported from al-Hasan and Zayd ibn 'Ali that they read "al-hamdi lillah" with a *kasra* on the *dal*, assimilating the second to the first.

Abu Ja'far ibn Jarir said: The meaning of ﴿al-hamdu lillah﴾ is gratitude to Allah alone, to the exclusion of all else that is worshipped besides Him and all that He has created, for the blessings He has bestowed upon His servants, which no number can count and no one other than Him can encompass. These include the soundness of the faculties for obedience and the enabling of the limbs of the bodies of the accountable (mukallafin) to perform His obligations, together with the provision He has spread for them in this world and the pleasant life He has nourished them with, without any entitlement on their part to it. They also include what He has made them aware of and called them to, of the means that lead to everlasting abode in the dwelling of permanence, in lasting bliss. So to our Lord belongs praise for all of that, first and last.

[Ibn Jarir also said: ﴿al-hamdu lillah﴾ is a praise with which He praised Himself, and implicit in it is that He commanded His servants to praise Him, as if He said: "Say: ﴿al-hamdu lillah﴾."] [[Addition from manuscripts ج، ط، أ، و.]]

He said: It has been said that the words of the speaker, "al-hamdu lillah," are praise of Him through His names and His attributes of beauty [[In manuscripts ج، ط، أ، و: "His beautiful names and His exalted attributes."]], and that the saying "ash-shukru lillah" is praise of Him for His blessings and favors. Then he began to refute this, with the upshot that all people of knowledge of the Arabic language use each of *al-hamd* and *ash-shukr* in place of the other [[In ج: "place."]].

[al-Sulami transmitted this view, that the two are identical, from Ja'far al-Sadiq and Ibn 'Ata' among the Sufis. Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿al-hamdu lillah﴾ is the word of every grateful person. al-Qurtubi cited in support of Ibn Jarir the correctness of the speaker's saying ﴿al-hamdu lillah﴾ as an expression of gratitude.] [[Tafsir al-Qurtubi (1/134). Addition from manuscripts ج، ط، أ، و.]]

What Ibn Jarir claimed is open to question, because it is well known among many later scholars that *al-hamd* is praise by speech for the one praised, for his necessary and transitive attributes, whereas *ash-shukr* only applies to transitive attributes, and it is expressed by the heart, the tongue and the limbs. As the poet said:

"Three things have benefited you from me: my hand, my tongue, and the hidden inner heart."

But they have differed as to which is more general, *al-hamd* or *ash-shukr*, on two views. The verified position is that there is a relation of general and specific between them. *Al-hamd* is more general than *ash-shukr* in terms of what they apply to, because it applies to both necessary and transitive attributes. You say: "I praised him for his horsemanship," and "I praised him for his generosity." But it is more specific, because it is only by speech. *Ash-shukr* is more general in terms of the means by which they are expressed, because it is by speech, action and intention, as has been mentioned. But it is more specific, because it only applies to transitive attributes. You do not say "I thanked him for his horsemanship," but you say "I thanked him for his generosity and his kindness to me." This is the summary of what some later scholars have written, and Allah knows best.

Abu Nasr Isma'il ibn Hammad al-Jawhari said: *al-hamd* is the opposite of blame. You say: "I praised the man, I praise him, praise [hamdan] and laudation [mahmadah], so he is *hamid* and *mahmud*." *Al-tahmid* is more emphatic than *al-hamd*, and *al-hamd* is more general than *ash-shukr*. About *ash-shukr* he said: it is praise of the benefactor for the kindness he has shown you, and one says "shakartuhu" and "shakartu lahu." The form with *lam* is more eloquent. [See Lisan al-'Arab by Ibn Manzur, root *h-m-d*.]

[As for *al-madh* (commendation), it is more general than *al-hamd*, because it can be for the living, the dead and also for inanimate things, as food and wealth are praised and the like. It can occur before a kindness and after it, and it applies to transitive and necessary attributes too, so it is more general.] [[Addition from manuscripts ج، ط، أ، و.]]

Mention of the sayings of the early generations (al-salaf) about *al-hamd*

Ibn Abi Hatim said: Abu Ma'mar al-Qati'i told us, Hafs told us, from Hajjaj, from Ibn Abi Mulaykah, from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: 'Umar said: "We know ﴿Subhan Allah﴾ and ﴿la ilaha illa Allah﴾, so what is ﴿al-hamdu lillah﴾?" 'Ali said: "It is a word with which Allah is pleased for Himself." [[Tafsir Ibn Abi Hatim (1/14).]]

Another narrator other than Abu Ma'mar related it from Hafs, saying: 'Umar said to 'Ali, with his companions present: "﴿La ilaha illa Allah﴾, ﴿Subhan Allah﴾, and ﴿Allahu akbar﴾, we know them, so what is ﴿al-hamdu lillah﴾?" 'Ali said: "A word which Allah loved for Himself, was pleased with for Himself, and loved to be said." [Al-Ashaj related it from Hafs but differed with him in it. The Hafiz's (Ibn Hajar's) treatment here suggests there is no contradiction. Ibn Abi Hatim said in his tafsir (1/15): "Thus Abu Ma'mar al-Qati'i related it from Hafs, and al-Ashaj told us, saying: 'Hafs told us,' but he differed from him in it, saying: 'Umar said to 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both, with his companions present: ﴿La ilaha illa Allah﴾, ﴿al-hamdu lillah﴾, ﴿Allahu akbar﴾, we know them, so what is ﴿Subhan Allah﴾? 'Ali said: "A word He loved for Himself, was pleased with for Himself, and loved to be said."' The Hafiz's words suggest there is no contradiction, so perhaps he saw it in another transmission, or perhaps it was an oversight, and Allah knows best.]

'Ali ibn Zayd ibn Ju'dan related from Yusuf ibn Mihran, who said: Ibn 'Abbas said: "﴿al-hamdu lillah﴾ is the word of gratitude, and when the servant says ﴿al-hamdu lillah﴾, He says: 'My servant has thanked Me.'" Ibn Abi Hatim related it.

He and Ibn Jarir also related, from the hadith of Bishr ibn 'Imarah, from Abu Rawq, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas, that he said: ﴿al-hamdu lillah﴾ is the thanking of Allah, humbling oneself before Him, acknowledging His blessings, His guidance, His beginning of favors, and other things.

Ka'b al-Ahbar said: ﴿al-hamdu lillah﴾ is the praise of Allah. al-Dahhak said: ﴿al-hamdu lillah﴾ is the mantle of the Most Merciful. A hadith has been transmitted with similar meaning.

Ibn Jarir said: Sa'id ibn 'Amr al-Sakuni told me, Baqiyyah ibn al-Walid told us, 'Isa ibn Ibrahim told me, from Musa ibn Abi Habib, from al-Hakam ibn 'Umayr, who had companionship (with the Prophet), who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When you say: ﴿al-hamdu lillahi rabbi al-'alamin﴾, you have thanked Allah, and He will increase you." [[Tafsir al-Tabari (1/136). Its isnad includes 'Isa ibn Ibrahim, of whom al-Bukhari said: "munkar al-hadith" (rejected in narration). His teacher Musa was declared weak by Abu Hatim and others, and al-Hakam ibn 'Umayr was described by Abu Hatim thus: "He narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ); he does not mention hearing or meeting him, and has rejected hadiths narrated from his nephew Musa ibn Abi Habib, who is a weak narrator in hadith, and 'Isa ibn Ibrahim narrates from Musa ibn Abi Habib, and he is one whose hadith is abandoned; I heard my father say that." End of quote, as drawn from the commentary of Allamah Ahmad Shakir on Tafsir al-Tabari.]

Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal narrated: Rawh told us, 'Awf told us, from al-Hasan, from al-Aswad ibn Sari', who said: I said: "O Messenger of Allah, shall I recite to you praises with which I have praised my Lord, blessed and exalted is He?" He said: "Indeed your Lord loves praise." [[Al-Musnad (3/435). al-Haythami said in al-Majma' (10/95): "Its narrators are the narrators of the Sahih," but it is *munqati'* (disconnected), since al-Hasan did not hear from al-Aswad, may Allah be pleased with him.]]

al-Nasa'i related it from 'Ali ibn Hujr, from Ibn 'Ulayyah, from Yunus ibn 'Ubayd, from al-Hasan, from al-Aswad ibn Sari', with the same wording. [Al-Sunan al-Kubra of al-Nasa'i, no. 7745.]

al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah related, from the hadith of Musa ibn Ibrahim ibn Kathir, from Talhah ibn Khirash, from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The best remembrance is ﴿la ilaha illa Allah﴾, and the best supplication is ﴿al-hamdu lillah﴾." [[Sunan al-Tirmidhi no. 3380; Sunan al-Nasa'i al-Kubra no. 10667; Sunan Ibn Majah no. 3800.]] al-Tirmidhi said: "Hasan gharib."

Ibn Majah related from Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah does not bestow a blessing upon a servant and he says ﴿al-hamdu lillah﴾, except that what He has given is better than what He has taken." [[Sunan Ibn Majah no. 3805, through Abu 'Asim, from Shabib ibn Bishr, from Anas. al-Busiri said in al-Zawa'id (3/192): "This isnad is good; Shabib ibn Bishr is disputed."] al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir, and in Nawadir al-Usul, from Anas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "If the world in its entirety were in the hand of a man of my community, and then he said ﴿al-hamdu lillah﴾, then ﴿al-hamdu lillah﴾ would be better than that." [[Al-Albani said in al-Silsilah al-Da'ifah (2/267): "Fabricated (mawdu')." It is narrated by Ibn 'Asakir (15/276/2) from Abu al-Mufaddal Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Muhammad ibn Hammam ibn al-Mutallib al-Shaybani, who said: al-Hafiz Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Hayy ibn Suwayd al-Harbi told me, Zurayq told us, 'Imran ibn Musa al-Jundaysaburi (resident of Bardha'ah) told us, Surah ibn Zuhayr al-Ghamiri (from the people of Basra) told us, Hushaym told me, from al-Zubayr ibn 'Adi, from Anas ibn Malik, as a marfu' report. This is fabricated, and its flaw is Abu al-Mufaddal. al-Khatib said (5/466, 467): "He used to narrate strange hadiths and questions of teachers, and people wrote from him on the recommendation of al-Daraqutni; then his lying became clear, so they tore up his hadiths and rejected his narrations. Afterwards he used to fabricate hadiths for the Rafidah." Hamzah ibn Muhammad ibn Tahir al-Daqqaq said: "He used to fabricate hadith, though he had an appearance of dignity and gravity." al-Azhari said to me: "Abu al-Mufaddal was a deceiver and a liar." Ibn 'Asakir related it from him in the biography of this Abu al-Mufaddal. As for those between him and Hushaym, I do not know them except Zurayq, and it appears he is Ibn Muhammad al-Kufi, who narrated from Hammad ibn Zayd. al-Dhahabi said: "Amir Ibn Makula declared him weak."]] al-Qurtubi and others said: That is, his inspiration to say ﴿al-hamdu lillah﴾ would be a greater blessing for him than the blessings of this world, because the reward of praise does not perish, while the bliss of this world does not last. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Wealth and children are the adornment of the life of this world, but the enduring good deeds are better with your Lord in reward and better in hope.﴾ [Al-Kahf: 46]. In the Sunan of Ibn Majah, from Ibn 'Umar: that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) related to them: "A servant of Allah's servants said: 'O my Lord, to You belongs praise as befits the majesty of Your Face and the greatness of Your dominion.' It stumped the two angels, so they did not know how to record it, so they ascended to heaven and said: 'O our Lord, a servant has uttered a statement we do not know how to record.' Allah, who knows best what His servant said, said: 'What did My servant say?' They said: 'O our Lord, he said: O my Lord, to You belongs praise as befits the majesty of Your Face and the greatness of Your dominion.' Allah said to them: 'Record it as My servant said, until he meets Me, and I will reward him for it.'" [[Sunan Ibn Majah no. 3801, through Sadaqah ibn Bishr from Qudamah ibn Ibrahim, from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both. al-Busiri said in al-Zawa'id (3/191): "This isnad has something to be said about it: Qudamah ibn Ibrahim was mentioned by Ibn Hibban among the trustworthy, and I have not seen anyone criticize or endorse Sadaqah ibn Bishr, and the rest of the narrators of the isnad are trustworthy."]]

al-Qurtubi reported from a group that they said: the servant's saying "al-hamdu lillahi rabbi al-'alamin" is better than the saying "la ilaha illa Allah," because "al-hamdu lillahi rabbi al-'alamin" includes monotheism together with praise. Others said: "La ilaha illa Allah" is better, because it is the distinction between faith and disbelief, and people are fought until they say "La ilaha illa Allah," as is established in the hadith agreed upon (Bukhari and Muslim), and in the other hadith in the Sunan: "The best thing I and the prophets before me have said is: 'La ilaha illa Allah, wahdahu la sharika lah'" [[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi in his Sunan no. 3585, through Hammad ibn Abi Humayd, from 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather. al-Tirmidhi said: "This is a gharib hadith from this route, and Hammad ibn Abi Humayd is Muhammad ibn Abi Humayd, Abu Ibrahim al-Ansari al-Madani, and he is not strong according to the people of hadith."]]. It has already been mentioned from Jabir, as a marfu' report: "The best remembrance is ﴿la ilaha illa Allah﴾, and the best supplication is ﴿al-hamdu lillah﴾." al-Tirmidhi graded it as hasan.

The alif and lam in "al-hamd" (all praise) are for comprehensiveness, encompassing every kind and category of praise, belonging to Allah, the Exalted, as is mentioned in the hadith: "O Allah, to You belongs all praise, to You belongs all sovereignty, in Your hand is all good, and to You all affairs return" (the hadith).[[Narrated from the hadith of Abu Sa'id and Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, may Allah be pleased with them both. As for the hadith of Abu Sa'id, al-Bayhaqi related it in Shu'ab al-Iman under no. (4400), by way of Khalid ibn Yazid, from Ibn Abi Dhi'b, from Zayd ibn Aslam, from 'Ata', from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri. As for the hadith of Sa'd, al-Bayhaqi related it in Shu'ab al-Iman under no. (4399), by way of Abu Balj, from Mus'ab ibn Sa'd, from his father Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas.]]

﴿Lord of the worlds﴾. The Rabb (Lord, Master) is the Owner who disposes of affairs. In the language it is used to mean the master (sayyid) and the one who manages things for their betterment, and all of these meanings are correct with respect to Allah, the Exalted.

[The word Rabb is not used for anyone other than Allah; rather, it is used with an attachment, as you say: "Rabb al-dar" (master of the house), "Rabb kadha" (master of such-and-such). As for Rabb on its own, it is not said except of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It has been said that it is the Greatest Name (al-Ism al-A'zam).][[Addition from J, T, A, W.]] . Al-'Alamin is the plural of 'alam (world), [and it is every existing thing other than Allah, Mighty and Majestic][[Addition from J, T, A, W.]], and "'alam" is a plural that has no singular from its own form. The 'awalim are the categories of created beings [in the heavens and the earth][[Addition from J, T.]], on land and in the sea. Each generation and age of them is also called an 'alam.

Bishr ibn 'Umarah related from Abu Rawq, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding ﴿All praise is for Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Fatihah: 2]: "All praise is for Allah, to whom belongs all creation: the heavens and the earths, and whoever is in them and what is between them, of what we know and of what we do not know."

And in the narration of Sa'id ibn Jubayr and 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas: "the Lord of jinn and mankind." Likewise said Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj, and it is related from 'Ali something similar.[[Addition from J, T, B, A, W.]] Ibn Abi Hatim said: it is with a chain that cannot be relied upon.

Al-Qurtubi used as evidence for this view the verse ﴿That he may be a warner to the worlds﴾ [al-Furqan: 1], meaning jinn and mankind. Al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubaydah said: "'alam" is an expression for that which has intellect, namely mankind, jinn, angels and devils, and "'alam" is not said of animals. And it is related from Zayd ibn Aslam and Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' [in W: "Abu Mahsin al-'Alim"] that "'alam" is everything that has a soul and is provided for. The hafiz Ibn 'Asakir mentioned in the biography of Marwan ibn Muhammad ibn Marwan ibn al-Hakam, who was the last of the caliphs of the Banu Umayyah, known as al-Ja'd and nicknamed al-Himar (the donkey), that he said: "Allah created seventeen thousand worlds; the people of the heavens and the people of the earth are one world, and the rest of them none knows [in W: "knows them"] except Allah, Mighty and Majestic."

Qatadah said: "Lord of the worlds," every kind is a world. Abu Ja'far al-Razi related from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, from Abu al-'Aliyah, regarding His saying ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾, that he said: "Mankind is one world, the jinn is one world, and beyond that are eighteen thousand worlds, or fourteen thousand worlds (he is uncertain), of angels upon the earth. The earth has four corners, and in each corner are three thousand worlds and five hundred worlds, which Allah created to worship Him." Related by Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim.

[This is a strange statement, and the like of it requires a sound proof.][[Addition from J, T.]]

Ibn Abi Hatim said: My father related to us, Hisham ibn Khalid related to us, al-Walid ibn Muslim related to us, al-Furat, meaning Ibn al-Walid, related to us, from Mu'attib [so it occurs in the copies, and in the original of Ibn Abi Hatim's Tafsir; in books of biography it occurs as "Mughith"] ibn Sumayy, from Tubay', meaning al-Himyari, regarding His saying ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾, he said: "The worlds are a thousand nations, six hundred in the sea and four hundred on land."

[Something similar is also reported from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib.][[Addition from J, T.]]

Something like this has also been related as a marfu' (traced to the Prophet) report, as the hafiz Abu Ya'la Ahmad ibn 'Ali ibn al-Muthanna said in his Musnad:

Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna related to us, 'Ubayd ibn Waqid al-Qays, Abu 'Abbad, related to us, Muhammad ibn 'Isa ibn Kaysan related to me, Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir related to us, from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: "Locusts became scarce in one of the years of 'Umar's rule, so he asked about them and was told nothing. He became distressed over that, so he sent a rider to Yemen, another to Syria, and another to Iraq, asking: 'Has any locust been seen or not?' He said: The rider who was from the direction of Yemen came to him with a handful of locusts, and threw them before him. When he saw them he said 'Allahu akbar,' then said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say:
"Allah created a thousand nations, six hundred in the sea and four hundred on land. The first of these nations to perish is the locust, and when it perishes, they follow one after another like beads when the string is cut." [[Ibn 'Adi related it in al-Kamil (5/352), (6/245), and al-Khatib in his Tarikh (11/218), by way of 'Ubayd ibn Waqid with similar wording. Ibn 'Adi said: "'Amr ibn 'Ali said: Muhammad ibn 'Isa is a Basran, the companion of Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir, weak, with rejected narrations; he narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir, from Jabir, from 'Umar, from the Prophet ﷺ about locusts." Ibn 'Adi also said: "'Ubayd ibn Waqid has no corroboration for this."]] Muhammad ibn 'Isa here, who is al-Hilali, is weak.

Al-Baghawi related from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib that he said: "For Allah there are a thousand worlds: six hundred in the sea and four hundred on land." Wahb ibn Munabbih said: "For Allah there are eighteen thousand worlds; this world is one of them." Muqatil said: "The worlds are eighty thousand." Ka'b al-Ahbar said: "None knows the number of the worlds except Allah, Mighty and Majestic." Al-Baghawi related all of this. Al-Qurtubi related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that he said: "Indeed for Allah there are forty thousand worlds; this world is one of them from its east to its west." Al-Zajjaj said: "The 'alam is everything that Allah created in this world and in the Hereafter." Al-Qurtubi said: "This is the correct view, that it encompasses all the worlds, as in His saying: ﴿Pharaoh said, 'And what is the Lord of the worlds?' He said, 'Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, if you are certain.'﴾" And 'alam is derived from 'alamah (sign). (I say): Because it is a sign that indicates the existence of its Creator, its Maker, and His oneness, as Ibn al-Mu'tazz said:

"How strange, how can the Deity be disobeyed,
or how can the denier deny Him?
And in everything there is a sign of His,
indicating that He is One."

And His saying: ﴿The Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾. The discussion of it has already been presented in the commentary on the basmalah (the invocation "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful"), in a manner that makes repeating it unnecessary.

Some readers recited: ﴿Malik yawm id-Din﴾ (Master of the Day of Judgment), and others recited: ﴿Maliki yawm id-Din﴾ (Owner of the Day of Judgment)[[In the manuscripts Jim, Ta, and Ba: "Some readers recited: 'Malik' and others recited: 'Malik'." (Malik / Maalik as variants.)]]. Both are authentic and mutawatir within the Seven (Readings).

[It is also said: Maliik. Nafi' lengthened the kasra of the kaf, reciting: "Malakiyy yawm id-Din." Scholars have preferred each of the two readings on semantic grounds, and both are sound and good. Al-Zamakhshari preferred Malik, because it is the reading of the people of the two Sanctuaries (Makkah and Madinah), and because of His saying: ﴿To whom belongs dominion this Day?﴾ and His saying: ﴿His word is the truth, and His is the dominion﴾. It is related from Abu Hanifah that he recited "Malaka yawma id-Din" as a verb with subject and object, but this is anomalous (shadhdh) and extremely strange][[Addition from manuscripts Jim, Ta, Alif, and Waw.]]. Abu Bakr ibn Abi Dawud related something strange on this point, saying: Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Adhrami related to us, 'Abd al-Wahhab related to us, from 'Adi[[In Ha: "'Abd al-Wahhab ibn 'Adi ibn al-Fadl."]] ibn al-Fadl, from Abu al-Mutarrif, from Ibn Shihab: that it reached him that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), Abu Bakr, 'Umar, 'Uthman, Mu'awiyah and his son Yazid ibn Mu'awiyah used to recite: ﴿Maliki yawm id-Din﴾, and the first to introduce "Maliki" was Marwan[[Al-Masahif by Ibn Abi Dawud (p. 104).]]. I say: Marwan had knowledge of the correctness of what he recited, which Ibn Shihab did not have access to, and Allah knows best.

It has been narrated through multiple chains, which Ibn Mardawayh cited, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to recite it: ﴿Maliki yawm id-Din﴾[[It was narrated by Abu Bakr ibn Abi Dawud in al-Masahif (p. 105) and al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak (2/232) through Ibn Fudayl from al-A'mash from Abu Salih, from Abu Hurayrah that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited: "Malik yawm id-Din." Ibn Abi Hatim added: "or he said: 'Maalik'." It was also narrated by Abu Bakr ibn Abi Dawud in al-Masahif (p. 105) and al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak (2/232) through Ibn Juraij from Ibn Abi Mulaykah from Umm Salamah that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to recite: "Malik yawm id-Din."]]. "Maalik" is derived from "mulk" (dominion), as He said: ﴿Indeed, We inherit the earth and whoever is upon it, and to Us they will be returned﴾ [Maryam: 40], and He said: ﴿Say, I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind, the King of mankind﴾ [an-Nas: 1, 2]. And "Malik" is derived from "al-mulk," as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿To whom belongs dominion this Day? To Allah, the One, the Subduer﴾ [Ghafir: 16], and He said: ﴿His word is the truth, and His is the dominion﴾ [al-An'am: 73], and He said: ﴿The dominion that Day belongs truly to the Most Merciful, and it will be a difficult day for the disbelievers﴾ [al-Furqan: 26].

Specifying dominion with the Day of Judgment does not negate it from anything else, because it has already been stated that He is "Lord of the worlds," which is general in this world and the Hereafter. He is attributed to the Day of Judgment because no one there claims anything, and no one speaks except by His permission, as He said: ﴿The Day when the Spirit and the angels stand in rows; none will speak except one whom the Most Merciful permits, and he will say what is correct﴾ [an-Naba': 38]. And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And voices will be hushed before the Most Merciful, so you will not hear except a whisper﴾ [Ta-Ha: 108], and He said: ﴿The Day it comes, no soul will speak except by His permission; so among them are the wretched and the happy﴾ [Hud: 105].

Al-Dahhak related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿Maliki yawm id-Din﴾ that he said: No one on that Day has any command with Him, as they had dominion in this world. He said: And the Day of Din is the Day of Reckoning for all creatures, which is the Day of Resurrection, when He will repay them for their deeds: if good, then good, and if evil, then evil, except whomever He pardons. Likewise said others among the Companions, the Successors, and the early scholars, and it is apparent.

Ibn Jarir related from some of them that he interpreted ﴿Maliki yawm id-Din﴾ as meaning the One Able to establish it, then he proceeded to weaken this view.

It is apparent that there is no contradiction between this view and what preceded it, and that each of those who held this and what came before acknowledges the validity of the other view and does not deny it. However, the context points more clearly to the first meaning than to this one, as He said: ﴿The dominion that Day belongs truly to the Most Merciful﴾ [al-Furqan: 26], and the second view resembles His saying: ﴿And the day He says "Be," and it is﴾ [al-An'am: 73]. And Allah knows best.

Al-Malik in reality is Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿He is Allah, other than whom there is no deity, the King, the Pure, the Source of Peace﴾. And in the two Sahihs, from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, as a marfu' report: "The most despised name before Allah is a man who names himself 'King of Kings' while there is no owner (malik) but Allah." And in both (Sahihs), from him, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "Allah will grasp the earth and fold the heaven with His right hand, then say: 'I am the King; where are the kings of the earth? Where are the tyrants? Where are the arrogant?'" And in the Great Qur'an: ﴿To whom belongs dominion this Day? To Allah, the One, the Subduer.﴾ As for naming others in this world "malik," it is by way of metaphor, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, Allah has sent to you Talut as king﴾, ﴿And there was behind them a king﴾, ﴿When He made among you prophets and made you kings﴾. And in the Two Sahihs: "[Like] kings upon thrones."

And ad-Din is recompense and reckoning, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿On that Day Allah will pay them their full due (din) in truth﴾, and He said: ﴿Are we indeed to be recompensed (madinun)?﴾, meaning: those who will be repaid and called to account. And in the hadith: "The wise one is he who holds himself accountable (dana nafsahu) and works for what comes after death," meaning he calls his soul to account for itself, as 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Call yourselves to account before you are called to account, weigh yourselves before you are weighed, and prepare for the Great Presentation, on the Day when none of your deeds is hidden: ﴿On that Day you will be presented, and no secret of yours will be concealed﴾."
