Commentary of Ibn Kathir (Tafsir al-Quran al-'Azim) on surah 1, verse 5:

The seven readers (al-Sab'ah, the seven canonical reciters) and the majority of readers recite the yaa' in ﴿iyyaka﴾ with a shaddah (doubled consonant). 'Amr ibn Fayid recited it without the shaddah, with a kasrah, but this is an anomalous (shadhdh) and rejected reading, because "iyya" means the sunlight. Some recited "ayyaka" with a fathah on the hamzah and a shaddah on the yaa', and some recited "hayyaka" with a haa' in place of the hamzah, as the poet said:

"So beware (fa-hayyaka) of the matter whose sources spread wide, yet whose outlets constrict you."

As for ﴿nasta'in﴾, all readers recite the nun at the beginning of the word with a fathah, except Yahya ibn Wathhab and al-A'mash, who recited it with a kasrah. This is the dialect of Banu Asad, Rabi'ah, Banu Tamim and Qays. [[Addition from manuscripts ج، ط، أ، و.]]

Worship ('ibadah) linguistically derives from humiliation (dhillah). It is said: a "mu'abbad" road, or a "mu'abbad" camel, meaning one made submissive (mudhallal). Technically, it is an expression that comprises the perfection of love, submission and fear.

The object, ﴿iyyaka﴾, is placed first and repeated, for emphasis (al-ihtimam) and restriction (al-hasr). That is, "We worship none but You, and we rely on none but You," and this is the perfection of obedience. All of religion returns to these two meanings. This is as some of the early scholars (al-Salaf) said: "Al-Fatihah is the secret of the Quran, and its secret is this phrase: ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾ [al-Fatihah: 5]." The first is a disavowal of shirk (associating partners with God), and the second is a disavowal of one's own power and strength, and entrusting oneself entirely to Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

This meaning appears in other verses of the Quran, as the Most High said: ﴿So worship Him and rely upon Him. And your Lord is not unaware of what you do﴾ [Hud: 123]; ﴿Say: He is the Most Merciful; we have believed in Him and upon Him we have relied﴾ [al-Mulk: 29]; ﴿Lord of the east and the west; there is no deity except Him, so take Him as Trustee﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 9]. Likewise this noble verse: ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾.

The discourse shifts from the third person (absence) to the second person (direct address) with the kaf of address, and this is appropriate, because when he praised Allah, it was as if he drew near and stood before Allah, the Most High. Therefore He said: ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾. This is evidence that the beginning of the surah is a report from Allah, the Most High, praising Himself with His noble attributes and His beautiful names, and a guidance to His servants that they should praise Him with that. For this reason the prayer of one who does not say this is not valid, while he is able to do so, as is reported in the two Sahihs (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim) from 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "There is no prayer for one who does not recite the Opening of the Book (Fatihah al-Kitab)." [[Sahih al-Bukhari no. (756) and Sahih Muslim no. (394).]] In Sahih Muslim, from the hadith of al-'Ala' ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, the freedman of al-Huraqah, from his father, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "Allah, the Most High, says: I have divided the prayer between Myself and My servant into two halves. Half of it is for Me and half of it is for My servant, and My servant shall have what he asks. When the servant says: ﴿All praise is for Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Fatihah: 2], He says: My servant has praised Me. When he says: ﴿The Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾ [al-Fatihah: 3], He says: My servant has extolled Me. When he says: ﴿Master of the Day of Judgement﴾ [al-Fatihah: 4], He says: My servant has glorified Me. When he says: ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾ [al-Fatihah: 5], He says: This is between Me and My servant, and My servant shall have what he asks. When he says: ﴿Guide us to the straight path, the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour, not of those who have evoked (Your) anger or of those who are astray﴾ [al-Fatihah: 6-7], He says: This is for My servant, and My servant shall have what he asks." [[Sahih Muslim no. (395).]]

Al-Dahhak reported from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿iyyaka na'budu﴾: it means "You alone we declare to be One (nuwahhid), and we fear and hope in You, O our Lord, not other than You." ﴿Wa iyyaka nasta'in﴾: "for help in Your obedience and in all our affairs."

Qatadah said regarding ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾: "He commands you to devote worship sincerely to Him, and to seek His help in your affairs."

The reason He placed ﴿iyyaka na'budu﴾ before ﴿wa iyyaka nasta'in﴾ is that worship of Him is the goal, while seeking help is a means to it. Concern and resolve consist in giving precedence to what is more important, then to what is next in importance. And Allah knows best.

If it is asked: what is the meaning of the nun in His saying ﴿iyyaka na'budu wa iyyaka nasta'in﴾? If it is for the plural, then the one calling is singular; and if it is for majesty (ta'zim), it does not suit this situation. It has been answered that what is meant by this is to report about the species of servants, and the one praying is one of them, especially if he is in a congregation or is their imam. So he reports about himself and his believing brothers (ikhwanihi) with the worship for which they were created, and he intercedes for them with what is good. Some of them said: it may be for majesty, as if it were said to the servant: "If you are in worship, you are noble and your standing is great, so say: ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾. But if you are outside of worship, do not say 'we' or 'we did,' even if you were among a hundred thousand or a million, because all are in need of Allah, Mighty and Majestic." Some of them said: "Iyyaka a'budu is more refined in humility than iyyaka na'budu, because in the second there is a glorification of oneself by making oneself alone worthy of worshipping Allah, the Most High, whom no one can worship as He deserves, nor praise Him as is fitting for Him. Worship is a great station (maqam 'azim) by which the servant is ennobled, for his affiliation to the court of Allah, the Most High, as one of them said:

"Do not call me except 'O slave of Her (or Him)', for that is the most noble of my names."

Allah named His Messenger "His servant" in his most noble stations, saying: ﴿Praise be to Allah, who sent down upon His servant the Book﴾ [al-Kahf: 1]; ﴿And when the servant of Allah stood up calling upon Him﴾ [al-Jinn: 19]; ﴿Glory be to He who took His servant by night﴾ [al-Isra': 1]. So He named him a servant at the time of the revelation's descent upon him, his standing in the call, and his night journey with him. He guided him to standing in worship at times when his chest was constricted by the denial of those who opposed him, where He says: ﴿And We know that your breast is constricted by what they say. So exalt your Lord with praise and be among the prostrators. And worship your Lord until there comes to you the certainty﴾ [al-Hijr: 97-99].

Fakhr al-Din (al-Razi) in his tafsir related from some people that the station of servanthood ('ubudiyyah) is more noble than the station of messengerhood (risalah), because worship proceeds from the creation to the Truth, while messengerhood proceeds from the Truth to the creation. He said: "And because Allah is the one who manages the welfare of His servant, while the Messenger manages the welfare of his community (ummah)." This statement is wrong, and this reasoning is also weak and has no substance. Fakhr al-Din did not criticise it with weakening nor reject it.

Some of the Sufis said: worship is either for obtaining reward and averting punishment. They said: this is of no value, since its aim is the attainment of its own goal. Or it is for the honour of bearing the obligations of Allah, the Most High, and this too is weak in their view. Rather, the higher level is to worship Allah for His sacred essence, described with perfection. They said: for this reason the one praying says, "I pray to Allah," and if it were for obtaining reward and averting punishment, his prayer would be invalid. Others refuted this and said: that worship is for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, does not contradict asking for a reward along with it, nor seeking to repel a punishment, as that Bedouin said: "As for me, I do not perform your chanting (dandanah) nor the chanting of Mu'adh. I only ask Allah for Paradise and seek refuge in Him from the Fire." The Prophet ﷺ said: "Around it we chant (hawlaha nudandin)." [[Reported by Ahmad in al-Musnad (3/474), Abu Dawud in al-Sunan no. (792), and Ibn Hibban in his Sahih no. (514), through the route of al-A'mash from Abu Salih from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]]

The reading of the majority is with the ṣād (ص). It was also read as "al-siraṭ" (السِّرَاط) and read with a zāy (ز). Al-Farrā' said: it is the dialect of Banū 'Udhra, Balqayn [[In A: "Balqīs".]] and Banū Kalb.

When the praise of the One being asked, tabāraka wa-ta'ālā (blessed and exalted is He), had preceded, it was fitting that it be followed by the request, as He said: "Half of it is for Me and half of it is for My servant, and My servant shall have what he asks." This is the most complete state of the one asking: that he praise the One he asks, then ask for his need [and the need of his fellow believers with his words: ﴿Guide us﴾] [[Addition from J, T, A, W.]], because this is more successful in attaining the need and more effective in obtaining a response. For this reason, God exalted be He, guided to it, since it is the most perfect. The request may be made by informing of the state of the one asking and his need, as Moses, peace be upon him, said: ﴿My Lord, I am truly in need of whatever good You send down to me﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ: 24]. It may also be preceded, along with that, by a description of the One being asked, like the saying of Dhū al-Nūn: ﴿There is no deity but You; glory be to You; I have indeed been of the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Anbiyā': 87]. It may also consist merely of praise of the One being asked, like the saying of the poet:

Shall I mention my need, or has your modesty sufficed me? Indeed, your nature is modesty.

If a man praises you one day, his praise suffices him from having to beg.

Guidance (al-hidāya) here means direction (al-irshād) and granting success (al-tawfīq). Guidance may be transitive by itself, as here: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾, so it implies the meaning of "inspire us," "grant us success," "provide for us," or "give us." ﴿And We showed him the two highways﴾ [al-Balad: 10], meaning: We made clear to him good and evil. It may also be followed by "ilā" (to), as in His saying: ﴿He chose him and guided him to a straight path﴾ [al-Naḥl: 121], ﴿So lead them to the path of Hellfire﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 23]. That is in the sense of direction and indication. Likewise His saying: ﴿And indeed you guide to a straight path﴾ [al-Shūrā: 52]. It may also be followed by "lām" (for), as in the saying of the people of Paradise: ﴿Praise be to God, who guided us to this﴾ [al-A'rāf: 43], meaning: He granted us success for this and made us worthy of it [[In T: "and made us worthy of it".]].

As for "al-ṣirāṭ al-mustaqīm" (the straight path), Imam Abū Ja'far Ibn Jarīr said: The nation of the people of interpretation (ta'wīl) all agreed that "the straight path" is the clear road in which there is no crookedness.

This is also the meaning in the language of all the Arabs. Among that is the saying of Jarīr ibn 'Aṭiyya al-Khaṭafī:

The Commander of the Believers is upon a path, straight when the watering places are crooked.

He said: The evidence for this is more than can be counted. He said: Then the Arabs borrow the word ṣirāṭ and use it for every saying and deed described as straight or crooked, so they describe the straight by its straightness and the crooked by its crookedness.

Then the expressions of the exegetes (mufassirūn) from the early generations (salaf) and later generations (khalaf) differed in explaining ṣirāṭ, although their conclusions return to one thing, which is following God and His Messenger. It was reported that it is the Book of God. Ibn Abī Ḥātim said: al-Ḥasan ibn 'Arafa narrated to us, Yaḥyā ibn Yamān narrated to me, from Ḥamza al-Zayyāt, from Sa'd, who is Abū [[In A and W: "Ibn".]] al-Mukhtār al-Ṭā'ī, from the nephew of al-Ḥārith al-A'war, from al-Ḥārith al-A'war, from 'Alī ibn Abī Ṭālib, may God be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "The straight path is the Book of God" [[Tafsīr Ibn Abī Ḥātim (1/20).]]. Likewise Ibn Jarīr narrated it from the hadith of Ḥamza ibn Ḥabīb al-Zayyāt, and it has already been mentioned in the chapter on the virtues of the Qur'an [[Aḥmad and al-Tirmidhī narrated it from the narration of al-Ḥārith al-A'war, from 'Alī, as a marfū' report: "And it is the firm rope of God, and it is the wise remembrance, and it is the straight path."]]. Ahmad and al-Tirmidhī narrated it from the narration of al-Ḥārith al-A'war, from 'Alī, as a marfū' (traced to the Prophet ﷺ): "And it is the firm rope of God, and it is the wise remembrance, and it is the straight path" [[Sunan al-Tirmidhī, no. (2906).]].

This has also been reported as a mawqūf (stopping at a Companion) from 'Alī, and it is more likely [[Al-Ṭabarī narrated it as mawqūf in his tafsīr (1/172). The discussion of this hadith has already preceded in the chapter on the virtues of the Qur'an.]], and God knows best.

Al-Thawrī said, from Manṣūr, from Abū Wā'il, from 'Abd Allāh (Ibn Mas'ūd), who said: The straight path is the Book of God. It was also said: it is Islam. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said, from Ibn 'Abbās, who said: Gabriel said to Muhammad, peace be upon them both: Say: O Muhammad, "Guide us to the straight path." He means: "Guide us [[In J, T, B, A, W: "and inspire us".]] to the guiding road, which is the religion of God in which there is no crookedness."

Maymūn ibn Mihrān said, from Ibn 'Abbās, regarding His saying: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾, he said: That is Islam. Ismā'īl ibn 'Abd al-Raḥmān al-Suddī al-Kabīr said, from Abū Mālik, and from Abū Ṣāliḥ, from Ibn 'Abbās, and from Murra al-Hamdānī, from Ibn Mas'ūd, and from some people among the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾, they said: It is Islam. 'Abd Allāh ibn Muḥammad ibn 'Aqīl said, from Jābir: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾, he said: It is Islam, and he said: It is wider than what is between the heaven and the earth. Ibn al-Ḥanafiyya said regarding His saying: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾, he said: It is the religion of God, which does not accept from the servants anything other than it. 'Abd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam said: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾, he said: It is Islam.

In the hadith narrated by Imam Aḥmad in his Musnad, where he said: al-Ḥasan ibn Sawwār Abū al-'Alā' narrated to us, Layth, that is Ibn Sa'd, narrated to us, from Mu'āwiya ibn Ṣāliḥ: that 'Abd al-Raḥmān ibn Jubayr ibn Nufayr narrated to him, from his father, from al-Nawwās ibn Sam'ān, from the Messenger of God ﷺ, who said: "God struck a parable of a straight path. On either side of the path are two walls in which there are open doors, and over the doors are lowered curtains. At the gate of the path is a caller who says: O people, enter the path all together and do not deviate. And a caller calls from above the path. When a person wants to open any of those doors, he says: Woe to you, do not open it, for if you open it you will enter it. So the path is Islam, the two walls are the limits of God, the open doors are the prohibitions of God, that caller at the head of the path is the Book of God, and the caller from above the path is the admonisher of God in the heart of every Muslim."

Likewise Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Ibn Jarīr narrated it from the hadith of Layth ibn Sa'd with it [[Al-Musnad (4/182), Tafsīr Ibn Abī Ḥātim (1/21), and Tafsīr al-Ṭabarī (1/176).]]. al-Tirmidhī and al-Nasā'ī both narrated it, from 'Alī ibn Ḥujr, from Baqiyya, from Bujayr [[In W: "Yaḥyā".]] ibn Sa'd, from Khālid ibn Ma'dān, from Jubayr ibn Nufayr, from al-Nawwās ibn Sam'ān, with it [[Sunan al-Tirmidhī, no. (2863), and Sunan al-Nasā'ī al-Kubrā, no. (11233).]].

This is a ṣaḥīḥ (sound) isnād, and God knows best.

Mujāhid said regarding ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾: he said: the truth. This is more comprehensive, and there is no contradiction between it and what preceded.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Ibn Jarīr narrated, from the hadith of Abū al-Naḍr Hāshim ibn al-Qāsim: Ḥamza ibn al-Mughīra narrated to us, from 'Āṣim al-Aḥwal, from Abū al-'Āliya, regarding ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾, he said: It is the Prophet ﷺ and his two companions after him. 'Āṣim said: We mentioned that to al-Ḥasan, and he said: Abū al-'Āliya spoke truly and gave good counsel.

All these sayings are correct, and they are interrelated, for whoever follows the Prophet ﷺ and emulates those after him, Abū Bakr and 'Umar, has followed the truth, and whoever follows the truth has followed Islam, and whoever follows Islam has followed the Qur'an, which is the Book of God, His firm rope, and His straight path. So all of them are correct, each confirming the others, and to God belongs praise.

Al-Ṭabarānī said: Muḥammad ibn al-Faḍl al-Saqaṭī narrated to us, Ibrāhīm ibn Mahdī al-Miṣṣīṣī narrated to us, Yaḥyā ibn Zakariyyā ibn Abī Zā'ida narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from Abū Wā'il, from 'Abd Allāh, who said: The straight path is the one upon which the Messenger of God ﷺ left us [[Al-Mu'jam al-Kabīr (10/245).]]. For this reason Imam Abū Ja'far Ibn Jarīr, may God have mercy on him, said: The most appropriate interpretation of this verse in my view, that is ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾, is that it means: grant us success in steadfastness upon what You have approved and what You granted success to those of Your servants upon whom You have bestowed favor, in speech and in action. That is the straight path, because whoever is granted success in what was granted to those upon whom God has bestowed favor among the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous, has been granted success in Islam, in confirming the messengers, in holding fast to the Book, in acting upon what God commanded, in refraining from what He forbade, in following the method of the Prophet ﷺ and the method of the four caliphs, and every righteous servant, and all of that is from the straight path.

If it is said: How does the believer ask for guidance at every time, in prayer and otherwise, while he is already characterized by it? Is this from the category of obtaining what is already obtained or not?

The answer: No. Had he not needed, night and day, to ask for guidance, God would not have directed him to that. The servant is in need at every moment and state of God, exalted be He, for His keeping him firm in guidance, for his rootedness in it, for his insight, for his increase in it, and for his persistence upon it, for the servant does not own for himself any benefit or harm except what God wills. So He, exalted be He, directed him to ask Him at every time to supply him with help, steadfastness, and success. The fortunate one is the one whom God grants success to ask Him, for He, exalted be He, has undertaken to respond to the one who calls upon Him, especially the one who is compelled, needy, and in want of Him at the hours of the night and the edges of the day. God, exalted be He, has said: ﴿O you who believe, believe in God and His Messenger and the Book that He sent down upon His Messenger and the Book that He sent down before﴾ [al-Nisā': 136], the verse. He commanded those who believe to believe, and there is no obtaining of what is already obtained in that, because what is intended is steadfastness, persistence, and continuity in the deeds that help toward that. And God knows best.

God, exalted be He, said, commanding His believing servants to say: ﴿Our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate after You have guided us, and grant us from Yourself mercy. Indeed, You are the Bestower﴾. And the Ṣiddīq, may God be pleased with him, used to recite this verse in the third rak'a of the Maghrib prayer after al-Fātiḥa, quietly. So the meaning of His saying: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ is: keep us steadfast upon it and do not divert us to other than it.

Ibn Kathir has already discussed the hadith about the servant who says ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ to the end of the surah, where Allah says: "This is for My servant, and My servant will have what he asks." His words ﴿the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾ explain ﴿the straight path﴾. Among the grammarians (al-nuhat), this phrase is a substitute (badal) for the earlier one, and it may also be an explicative apposition (ʿatf bayan). Allah knows best.

﴿Those upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾ are those mentioned in Surat an-Nisa, where He says: ﴿And whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger, those are with the ones upon whom Allah has bestowed favour, of the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous. And excellent are those as companions. That is the bounty from Allah, and sufficient is Allah as Knower.﴾ [An-Nisa: 69-70]

Al-Dahhak reported from Ibn Abbas: "The path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour" means those who were favoured by Your obedience and worship, from among Your angels, Your prophets, the truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous. This is similar to what our Lord, exalted is He, said: ﴿And whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger, those are with the ones upon whom Allah has bestowed favour﴾ and so on [An-Nisa: 69].

Abu Ja'far reported from al-Rabi' ibn Anas: "﴿The path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾ — they are the prophets." Ibn Juraij reported from Ibn Abbas: "They are the believers," and Mujahid said the same. Waki' said: "They are the Muslims." Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam said: "They are the Prophet ﷺ and those with him." The explanation previously narrated from Ibn Abbas is more general and more comprehensive. Allah knows best.

* *

As for His words, exalted is He: ﴿Not the path of those who have evoked (Your) anger, nor of those who are astray﴾. The majority of reciters (al-Jumhur) read "ghayri" with a kasra, as an adjective (naʿt). Al-Zamakhshari said: It has also been read with a fatha, as a circumstantial accusative (ḥal). This is the reading of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and of ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, and it is also related from Ibn Kathir. The one who is qualified (dhu al-ḥal) is the pronoun in ﴿upon them﴾, and the governing word (al-ʿamil) is ﴿You have bestowed﴾. The meaning is: "Guide us to the straight path, the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour, from among those whose description and attributes have been mentioned, who are the people of guidance, uprightness, and obedience to Allah and His messengers, and of carrying out His commands and abstaining from His prohibitions and restraints, not the path of those upon whom wrath has been evoked, who are those whose wills were corrupted: they knew the truth and deviated from it; nor the path of those who are astray, who are those who lacked knowledge, so they wander in error and are not guided to the truth." The statement was emphasised with "lā" (nor) to indicate that there are two corrupt ways, namely the ways of the Jews and the Christians.

Some grammarians claimed that ﴿ghayr﴾ here is exceptive (istithnaʾiyya), so that it would be discontinuous (munqaṭiʿ), since they are excluded from those upon whom favour was bestowed, and they are not among them. But what we have presented is more appropriate, based on the words of the poet [this is al-Nabigha al-Dhubyani, and the verse is in Tafsir al-Tabari (1/179)]:

"As if you were a camel from the camels of Banu Uqaysh,
Clattering near its legs with a water-skin."

That is: "As if you were a camel from the camels of Banu Uqaysh," where the qualified noun was omitted and the adjective was retained. Likewise: ﴿not of those upon whom wrath has been evoked﴾.
